title: The Requirement of (at least) Complex Structure for Quantum Mechanics
abstract: It is argued that many real-valued constructions of quantum mechanics are only \emph{nominally} real in that the operators and states are restricted to impose a \emph{complex structure} on the Hilbert space. That is, complex algebra between pairs of elements representing complex numbers is preserved in these formulations. It is therefore mistaken to think of these constructions as being `real' as they are actually a representation of complex linear algebra. It is then shown that under the assumptions of state normalisation and strict energy conservation, this complex structure (at the very least) is required to allow for time evolution in quantum mechanics. This is only a \emph{minimum} requirement, as our arguments do not preclude the formulation of quantum mechanics in terms of hyper-complex entities, such as quaternions.
summary: This paper argues that quantum mechanics fundamentally requires a complex structure, even if one attempts to formulate it using only real numbers. By analyzing the constraints imposed by energy conservation and state normalization on real matrix representations, the authors demonstrate that the complex algebra is mathematically necessary for time evolution. It serves as a foundational mathematical critique of 'real' quantum theories.
main_problem: The paper investigates the fundamental mathematical requirements for formulating quantum mechanics, specifically arguing that any such formulation, even those appearing real-valued, must inherently rely on a complex structure.
main_result: Under standard assumptions like state normalization and energy conservation, the complex structure is shown to be a minimum requirement for time evolution in quantum mechanics.
